text:
T: So, how have you been since we met last week?
P: Honestly, pretty rough. I ran out of my medication for a few days.
T: Oh no, what happened there?
P: The pharmacy said my refill wasn't authorized yet, so I had to wait.
T: That sounds stressful. How did you feel during those days without it?
P: My anxiety was through the roof. I couldn't sleep at all.
T: I'm sorry to hear that. Did you notice any other symptoms coming back?
P: Yeah, the racing thoughts came back, and I started avoiding people again.
T: Let's come back to that avoidance in a minute. First, is the medication sorted out now?
P: Yes, I picked it up yesterday, so I'm back on track.
T: Good. How are you feeling today, now that you're back on it?
P: A little better, but still shaky. Like I'm waiting for something bad to happen.
T: That makes sense after a disruption like that. Can you tell me more about the avoidance you mentioned?
P: I skipped my sister's birthday dinner. I just couldn't face being around people.
T: What went through your mind when you thought about going?
P: That everyone would notice something was off with me, that I'd embarrass myself.
T: That's a thought we've talked about before - the idea that others are watching closely and judging.
P: Right, the same old story.
T: Did you try any of the strategies we practiced, like checking the evidence for that thought?
P: I tried a little, but I was too tired to really do it properly.
T: That's understandable given the week you had. Let's practice it together now if that's okay.
P: Sure.
T: What evidence do you have that people were watching you closely at past events?
P: I guess... no one has ever actually said anything negative to me.
T: So the fear is more about what you imagine than what's actually happened.
P: When you put it that way, yeah.
T: How did it feel just now, walking through that?
P: A bit calmer, honestly. Still nervous, but calmer.
T: Great, that's good practice. Now, let's talk about your sleep. You mentioned it was bad this week.
P: I was lying awake for hours, just replaying conversations in my head.
T: Any particular conversation that kept coming back?
P: One with my boss. She asked why a report was late and I spiraled from there.
T: What was the spiral like?
P: I kept thinking I was about to get fired, that I'm failing at everything.
T: That's a big jump from one late report to failing at everything.
P: I know it sounds extreme when I say it out loud.
T: What would you say to a friend who had that same thought about their job?
P: I'd tell them one late report doesn't mean they're failing.
T: Can you offer yourself that same compassion?
P: I can try.
T: Let's set that as a small goal for this week - noticing when you jump to the worst case and pausing.
P: Okay, I can do that.
T: How has your mood been otherwise, on a scale of one to ten?
P: Maybe a four. It's been a low week overall.
T: What's contributed to the four, aside from the medication gap?
P: Work has been overwhelming, and I haven't been exercising like I planned.
T: We talked about exercise helping your mood before. What got in the way this week?
P: Honestly, just low motivation. I'd plan to go and then just not.
T: That's common when mood dips. Would a smaller goal feel more manageable, like a ten minute walk?
P: Yeah, that feels less overwhelming.
T: Let's put that in the plan too - a ten minute walk at least three times this week.
P: Okay.
T: Have you been using the breathing exercises we practiced for the anxiety?
P: A couple times, when it got really bad at night.
T: Did they help at all?
P: A little. It didn't stop the thoughts, but it slowed my heart rate down.
T: That's actually a really good sign - the physical calming can create space to work with the thoughts.
P: I didn't think of it that way.
T: Let's talk about your relationship with your sister. You mentioned missing her birthday.
P: I feel guilty about that. I haven't even texted her an apology.
T: What's stopping you from reaching out?
P: I'm scared she's mad at me and doesn't want to hear from me.
T: Has she given you any indication of that?
P: No, actually she texted me yesterday just checking in.
T: That sounds like she's not upset at all.
P: Yeah, I guess I was projecting again.
T: What would it look like to send her a short message today?
P: I could just say I'm sorry I missed it and that I love her.
T: That sounds like a good, manageable step. Can you commit to sending that today?
P: Yes, I'll do it after this.
T: Good. Let's shift to talk about work stress a bit more. How many hours have you been working?
P: Probably sixty this week. I keep taking on extra projects.
T: Why do you think you keep taking on more than you can handle?
P: If I say no, I'm afraid they'll think I'm not capable.
T: That fear of being seen as incapable comes up a lot for you.
P: It really does. I think it goes back to my dad always pushing me to do more.
T: That's an important connection. How did that pressure show up growing up?
P: Nothing was ever good enough. Even A's needed to be A pluses.
T: So the belief that you have to overperform to be valued started early.
P: Yeah, I never really thought about where it came from until now.
T: How does it feel to recognize that pattern?
P: Kind of sad, honestly. Like I've been carrying this a long time.
T: That's a really valuable insight for us to keep working on.
P: Thank you for pointing it out.
T: Let's talk briefly about your support system. Who do you feel you can lean on right now?
P: My sister, and maybe one friend from college, Maya.
T: Have you talked to Maya about how you've been feeling?
P: Not in detail. I usually just say I'm fine.
T: What keeps you from opening up more with her?
P: I don't want to burden her with my problems.
T: Do you think she'd see it as a burden?
P: Probably not. She's always been pretty understanding.
T: Might be worth testing that belief by sharing a little more next time you talk.
P: I could try that.
T: As we wrap up, let's review what we covered today and set the plan for next week.
P: Okay.
T: You'll text your sister today, aim for three short walks this week, and practice catching the worst-case thinking.
P: That sounds doable.
T: And maybe try opening up a bit more with Maya if the opportunity comes up.
P: I'll try.
T: How are you feeling about the session overall?
P: Better than when I walked in, honestly. A bit more hopeful.
T: I'm glad to hear that. Same time next week?
P: Yes, that works for me.
T: Great, take care of yourself, and I'll see you then.
P: Thanks, see you next week.

T: Welcome back. How was your week?
P: It was okay, but I had another panic attack on Tuesday.
T: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you walk me through what happened?
P: I was at the grocery store and suddenly felt like I couldn't breathe.
T: What do you think triggered it?
P: The store was really crowded, and I started feeling trapped.
T: That sounds frightening. What did you do in the moment?
P: I left my cart and rushed outside to the parking lot.
T: Did leaving help you feel better?
P: Yes, almost immediately, but then I felt embarrassed about leaving my cart.
T: That's a common pattern - escape brings relief but also guilt afterward.
P: Exactly. I keep replaying it in my head.
T: Let's look at the panic cycle we talked about before. What was the first physical sensation you noticed?
P: My chest got tight and my heart started racing.
T: And what thought came right after that sensation?
P: That I was going to pass out or have a heart attack.
T: That thought then fuels more physical symptoms, which fuels more fear.
P: Yeah, it spirals really fast.
T: Did you try the grounding technique we practiced?
P: I forgot about it in the moment, honestly.
T: That's okay, it takes practice before it becomes automatic. Want to review it now?
P: Yes please.
T: Let's start with naming five things you can see around you right now.
P: A window, a plant, your notebook, a clock, and my own hands.
T: Good. How does your body feel after doing that?
P: A little calmer, actually. My shoulders dropped a bit.
T: That's the grounding working. Try to use that the next time you feel the panic starting.
P: I'll try to remember this time.
T: Let's also talk about avoidance. Have you been avoiding the grocery store since then?
P: Yes, my partner has been going instead.
T: How do you feel about relying on him for that?
P: Guilty, but also relieved I don't have to go.
T: Avoidance often feels relieving short term but can make the fear stronger long term.
P: I know, we've talked about this with other things too.
T: Would you be willing to try a small exposure step this week?
P: Maybe. What would that look like?
T: Perhaps going to a smaller, less crowded store for just a few minutes.
P: That feels more manageable than the big one.
T: Let's plan for you to try that, maybe with your partner waiting in the car nearby for support.
P: Okay, I can try that on Thursday.
T: Good. Now, how have things been with your partner otherwise?
P: Pretty good, actually. We had a nice weekend together.
T: I'm glad to hear that. What did you do?
P: We went hiking and just talked a lot. It felt normal, like before all this started.
T: That sounds really positive. Did you notice less anxiety during that time?
P: Yes, being outside and moving really does help.
T: We've noticed that pattern before too - activity seems to lower your anxiety baseline.
P: I should probably do more of that instead of sitting around worrying.
T: What's made it hard to do more of that during the week?
P: Work has been busy, and by the time I get home I just want to collapse.
T: That makes sense. Even a short walk after work might help without draining you too much.
P: I could try a fifteen minute walk after dinner.
T: Let's add that as a goal. How's your sleep been this week?
P: Better than before, maybe six hours a night.
T: That's an improvement. What do you think helped?
P: I stopped looking at my phone right before bed like you suggested.
T: That's great follow-through. How did that feel to change?
P: Hard at first, but now it's becoming a habit.
T: I'm proud of you for sticking with it. Let's talk about work stress now.
P: There's a big presentation coming up next month that I'm already dreading.
T: What specifically worries you about it?
P: That I'll freeze up or panic in front of everyone.
T: Has that happened before in a presentation?
P: Once, years ago, and I've never fully gotten over it.
T: That one experience seems to have left a strong mark.
P: Yeah, I still think about it sometimes.
T: What happened exactly, if you're comfortable sharing?
P: I blanked out mid-sentence and just stood there for what felt like forever.
T: That must have been really distressing at the time.
P: It was humiliating. I thought everyone was judging me.
T: Do you know how people actually reacted?
P: Someone helped me find my place again, and it was fine after that, but I only remember the bad part.
T: That's interesting - the memory got stuck on the worst moment rather than the resolution.
P: I never thought about it that way.
T: Would it help to prepare some grounding strategies specifically for this presentation?
P: Yes, that would help me feel less scared going in.
T: Let's plan to spend part of next session preparing for that specifically.
P: That sounds really helpful, thank you.
T: Of course. How has your mood been overall this week, one to ten?
P: I'd say a six, which is better than last time.
T: That's good progress. What do you think contributed to the improvement?
P: Sleeping better and the good weekend with my partner, I think.
T: Those both sound like meaningful factors. Let's keep tracking what helps and what doesn't.
P: Okay, I'll keep a note of it.
T: Have you been taking your medication consistently?
P: Yes, every day, no issues there.
T: Good, that consistency is important. Any side effects to report?
P: Just a bit of dry mouth, nothing major.
T: Let's keep an eye on that, but it doesn't sound concerning right now.
P: Okay.
T: Let's recap the plan for this week. Try the small grocery store exposure on Thursday.
P: Got it.
T: Add a fifteen minute walk after dinner a few times this week.
P: Okay.
T: And keep practicing the grounding technique, even outside of panic moments, so it feels more natural.
P: I can do that.
T: How are you feeling about everything we discussed today?
P: Good, a little more hopeful about the presentation too.
T: I'm glad. You've made real progress these past few weeks.
P: Thank you, it helps to hear that.
T: Same time next week to check in and start preparing for the presentation?
P: Yes, that works great.
T: Perfect, take care until then.
P: Thanks, you too. See you next week.

T: Good to see you again. Before we start, how are you feeling right now, coming into today?
P: A bit tense, actually. I had a hard conversation with my roommate this morning.
T: Thanks for telling me. Let's make sure that gets a spot on today's agenda. What else would you like to cover?
P: The roommate thing, definitely. And I wanted to talk about work - my manager keeps piling things on me.
T: Okay. I'd also like to review the thought record from last week, and I was thinking we could practice the assertiveness skill we talked about. Does that sound alright?
P: Yes, that sounds good.
T: We have about fifty minutes. Which of these feels most pressing to you?
P: Probably the roommate. It's what's on my mind the most.
T: Then let's start with a quick homework review, then the roommate situation, and use that as the basis for the assertiveness practice. If we have time, we'll look at work. Does that order work for you?
P: Yes, that makes sense.
T: Before we dive in, I wanted to ask how you felt about last session. Was there anything that didn't sit well with you?
P: It was helpful, though I felt a bit rushed at the end when we set the homework.
T: That's really useful to hear, thank you. I'll make sure we leave more time at the end today. Please tell me if that happens again.
P: Okay, I will.
T: So, the thought record. How did it go?
P: I filled it out three times. Twice about work, once about my roommate.
T: That's great effort. What did you notice when you looked back over them?
P: The same thought kept showing up - that if I say what I want, people will get angry and leave.
T: So the main conclusion was that a belief about other people getting angry runs through all three situations.
P: Yes, exactly.
T: That links up with what we've been calling your core fear of rejection. It seems to drive a lot of the giving in.
P: It really does.
T: Let's turn to this morning. What happened with your roommate?
P: She's been leaving dishes in the sink for a week. I wanted to say something but I just cleaned them instead.
T: What went through your mind when you thought about bringing it up?
P: That she'd think I'm petty and start resenting me.
T: How strongly did you believe that, zero to a hundred?
P: Maybe eighty.
T: And how did you feel while you were cleaning the dishes?
P: Angry, and kind of hopeless. Like this is how it's always going to be.
T: So the thought "she'll resent me" leads to staying quiet, and staying quiet leads to anger building up.
P: Yeah, I've never really seen it laid out like that.
T: Let me check I've got this right. You avoid saying something to protect the friendship, but the resentment ends up building on your side instead. Is that accurate, or would you put it differently?
P: That's accurate. Maybe I'd add that I also feel like a doormat.
T: Thanks for adding that. Feeling like a doormat is an important part of this. Has your roommate ever reacted badly when you've asked for something before?
P: Not really. Once I asked her to turn the music down and she just said sorry.
T: So there's at least one piece of evidence that doesn't fit the prediction that she'll resent you.
P: I guess that's true.
T: This is a good place to practice assertiveness. The reason I suggest it is that you've told me your goal is to feel more respected in your relationships, and being able to make a clear, calm request is a skill that builds directly toward that.
P: Okay. I'm nervous, but I see why it would help.
T: Let's go through the steps first. One, describe the situation without blaming. Two, say how it affects you. Three, make a specific request. Four, check in with the other person. I'll show you first. I'll be you and you be your roommate.
P: Okay.
T: "Hey, I've noticed the dishes have been piling up in the sink this week. It's been stressing me out when I come home. Would you be able to wash yours by the end of each day? Does that work for you?"
P: That sounds so calm. I'd say, "Oh, sorry, I've been really busy."
T: Then I might say, "I understand, things have been hectic. Maybe we could figure out a system that works for both of us." Now let's switch. You be you, and I'll be your roommate.
P: Okay. Um, "Hey, so the dishes... they've kind of been in the sink a lot. Sorry to bring it up."
T: Let's pause there. What did you notice about how that went?
P: I apologized. And I didn't actually ask for anything.
T: You noticed that yourself, which is great. You also named the situation clearly and kept a friendly tone - that's exactly step one. One suggestion: leave out the "sorry" and add a specific request at the end. Want to try again?
P: "Hey, I've noticed the dishes have been piling up. It's been stressing me out. Could you wash yours by the end of each day?"
T: That's much stronger. You described it, said how it affects you, and made a clear request, all without apologizing. How did that feel?
P: Weird, but good. Like I'm allowed to ask.
T: Let's do it one more time and add step four, checking in with her.
P: "Hey, I've noticed the dishes have been piling up, and it's been stressing me out. Could you wash yours by the end of each day? Does that seem fair to you?"
T: Excellent. You added the check-in smoothly, and your voice was steadier that time. On a scale of zero to a hundred, how much do you believe she'll resent you now?
P: Maybe fifty. Lower than before.
T: That's a big shift. How do you feel compared to when you first came in?
P: Less tense. A bit more confident.
T: We have about fifteen minutes left. Do you want to briefly touch on work, or spend the time planning for the conversation with your roommate?
P: Let's plan for the roommate. Work can wait until next week.
T: Okay, we'll put work first on next week's agenda. For homework, I'd like you to have this conversation with your roommate sometime in the next three days, using the four steps. Before you do it, write down how much you believe she'll resent you, and afterwards write down what actually happened.
P: Okay.
T: The point is to test the prediction directly, not just in theory. It gives us real evidence to work with next session.
P: That makes sense.
T: Can you think of anything that might get in the way of doing it?
P: She works late on weekdays, so I might chicken out and say there was no good time.
T: That's a realistic obstacle. What could you do about it?
P: I could text her to ask when she's free for a quick chat on Saturday morning.
T: That's a great solution. Let's write that down too. Is there anything else that might make it hard?
P: If she gets defensive, I might back down.
T: If that happens, what's one thing you could say from what we practiced?
P: "I understand, maybe we can figure out a system that works for both of us."
T: Perfect. You've got a plan for that too. Before we finish, what's your feedback on today's session?
P: It was really helpful. The role play felt awkward at first, but it's the most practical thing we've done.
T: Thanks for being honest about the awkwardness. Was there anything you didn't like, or would want done differently?
P: Maybe a bit less time on the homework review next time, so we have more time for practice.
T: That's fair. I'll keep the review shorter next week. Did we leave enough time for the homework today?
P: Yes, much better than last time.
T: Good. To sum up: you'll text your roommate to set a time, have the conversation using the four steps, and record your prediction and what actually happened.
P: Got it.
T: Great work today. See you next week.
P: Thanks, see you then.

T: Hi, come in. So what's going on?
P: Not great. I've been feeling really down this past week.
T: Mm. Okay. Did you do the worksheet I gave you?
P: I forgot about it, honestly.
T: Right. Well, let's just talk then. What's been happening?
P: My girlfriend and I broke up on Saturday.
T: Oh. That's tough. These things happen though.
P: I guess. It just feels like the end of the world right now.
T: Well, it's not the end of the world. You'll meet someone else.
P: Maybe. It doesn't feel like it.
T: How long were you together?
P: Three years.
T: That's a while. Whose idea was it to end it?
P: Hers. She said I was too closed off and never talked about my feelings.
T: Do you think that's true?
P: Maybe. I don't know. I always thought I was fine.
T: A lot of men struggle with that. It's pretty common.
P: Okay.
T: Have you been sleeping?
P: Not much. I keep waking up at 3am thinking about her.
T: You should try melatonin. A lot of people find it helps.
P: Maybe.
T: And cut out caffeine after lunch. That makes a big difference.
P: I only have one coffee in the morning.
T: Well, it's still worth looking at. How's work?
P: I called in sick twice this week. I couldn't face it.
T: You don't want to make a habit of that. You could lose your job.
P: I know. I'm worried about that too.
T: So try to get in every day this week, even if you don't feel like it.
P: I'll try.
T: Have you been seeing friends?
P: Not really. I don't want them to see me like this.
T: Why not?
P: They'll think I'm pathetic for being this upset over a breakup.
T: I'm sure they won't think that. Friends are supposed to support you.
P: Maybe.
T: What about exercise? You used to go to the gym.
P: I haven't been in months.
T: It's really good for depression. You should start going again.
P: It's hard to get motivated.
T: Everyone finds it hard. You just have to push through.
P: Yeah.
T: Do you have any family nearby?
P: My brother lives about an hour away.
T: Could you visit him this weekend?
P: Maybe. We're not that close.
T: It could still be good to get out of the house.
P: I suppose.
T: Let me ask you something. When you think about the breakup, what goes through your head?
P: That I ruin every relationship. That something's wrong with me.
T: That sounds pretty harsh on yourself.
P: It's how I feel.
T: Well, it takes two people for a relationship to end.
P: She didn't do anything wrong, though. It was me.
T: I doubt it was all you.
P: You weren't there.
T: True. Anyway. How's your appetite?
P: I'm not really eating much. Mostly snacks.
T: Try to eat proper meals. Your body needs it.
P: Okay.
T: Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself?
P: No, nothing like that.
T: Good. If you ever do, call the crisis line or go to the emergency room.
P: Okay.
T: What else? Anything else you wanted to talk about?
P: I don't know. I'm just tired all the time.
T: That's probably the poor sleep. Try the melatonin.
P: Alright.
T: So, um, I think what we should do, or what might be good, is, well - let's think about some things you could do this week.
P: Okay.
T: Get back to the gym, maybe see your brother, and try to get to work every day.
P: That's a lot.
T: Just do what you can.
P: Okay.
T: And try the worksheet again if you get time.
P: Which one was it again?
T: The one with the columns. You'll find it.
P: Okay.
T: Alright, we're about out of time. Same time next week?
P: Sure.
T: Okay. Take care.
P: Bye.
